```diff
author: magent-cryptograss
body:
Fixes #17.

## What was happening

`getMwn()` logged in once and handed back the same client forever. MediaWiki expires the session behind it after `$wgObjectCacheSessionExpiry` — an hour by default — and a cookie-holding client has no way to know. It keeps making requests, the server keeps treating them as anonymous, and the edit comes back:

```
permissiondenied: limited to users in the group: Users
```

That message reads as a problem with the bot account's rights, which is why this got misdiagnosed twice. Most recently I told Justin the redeploy had logged the MCP out — no deploy was involved; the process was just 26 hours old.

## The check is free

Signing a write already costs a round trip for a CSRF token, and MediaWiki hands an unrecognised client the token `+\` — two characters, where a real one is a long hex string. Confirmed against pickipedia.xyz:

```
$ curl -s 'https://pickipedia.xyz/api.php?action=query&meta=tokens&format=json'
anon csrftoken repr: '+\\' len 2
```

So "am I still logged in?" is answered by a response we were already waiting for. **Reads pay nothing** — they carry no token, so there is nothing to check them against, and they keep the old path.

## Why a new client instead of `login()`

mwn already has re-login logic for `assertuserfailed`, but it reuses the cookie jar, and MediaWiki refuses a BotPassword login that arrives carrying a BotPassword session:

```
Cannot log in when using MediaWiki\Session\BotPasswordSessionProvider sessions.
```

The bot authenticates as `Magent@magent`, a BotPassword, so that is the ordinary case here. A fresh client starts with an empty jar and cannot hit it.

## Two supporting changes

- **Cache the login promise, not the resolved client.** Two concurrent tools could both find the cache empty and both log in. Tolerable when it only happened at startup; not once a stale session can trigger a login mid-run.
- **Read cookies after re-authenticating, not before.** The old `withAuth()` fetched cookies and then the token. Recovery replaces the cookie jar, so fetching first would pair the dead session's cookies with a freshly minted token — the same failure, harder to see.

## Verification

`scripts/check-reauth.mjs`, run against the live wiki. It reproduces the production condition precisely: log in, capture the cookies, log out to destroy the server-side session, then put the still-valid-looking cookies back. Emptying the jar would be a much weaker test, because an empty jar is an obvious problem and is not what production leaves behind.

```
Baseline:
  ok    logs in — as Magent
  ok    writes are authenticated — probing "Basic Folk"

After the session expires:
  ok    server no longer recognises the cookies — sees 172.18.0.1
  ok    getAuthenticatedSession logs back in
  ok    it builds a fresh client rather than reusing the dead one
  ok    writes are authenticated again

Healthy sessions are left alone:
  ok    no needless second login

Concurrent callers share one recovery:
  ok    all three recover
  ok    and share a single client
```

Run it with `CONFIG=/path/to/config.json node scripts/check-reauth.mjs`. It is deliberately **not** wired into `npm test` — it needs real credentials, and there is nothing to stub that would still be testing the thing that broke.

The write probe sends a stale `latest.id`, so nothing is ever saved; what distinguishes pass from fail is *which* objection comes back. Being turned down over the revision id means authentication got through. It discovers an editable page rather than hardcoding one, and refuses to run if a healthy session can't produce a clean baseline — otherwise a missing or protected page would report a working fix as broken. That happened during development and is why the guard is there.

**Control run against `master`, same script, same dead session:** `DENIED as anonymous`. The test can see the bug.

`npm test` and `npm run lint` both clean (the two remaining warnings are pre-existing, in `config.ts`).

## After merging

Per the usual trap — merging isn't shipping. `git pull` → `npm run build` → **restart the MCP server**, in that order.

author: mc-nv
body:
## Description

Enables the NVIDIA `secret-scan-trufflehog` pre-commit hook, pinned to `v0.3.0`,
as the first entry under `repos:` so scanning runs before any formatter rewrites
the working tree.

This adopts the centrally maintained hook published by `NVIDIA/security-workflows`
rather than a hand-rolled TruffleHog invocation, so the scanner version and its
per-platform checksums are bumped in one reviewed place instead of 27.

`v0.3.0` is pinned deliberately. It installs the scanner inside pre-commit's own
Python environment — removing the shell installer, so Windows works without Git
Bash — and it adds `--exclude-detectors=lob`. That exclusion matters here: a Lob
API key is `test_` followed by 35 characters, so the detector matches ordinary
pytest function names such as `test_gpu_conf_compute_attestation_report`, and
Lob's verifier reports them as *verified* — the one result class this hook fails
on.

Behaviour: scans only the files pre-commit supplies (staged files at commit time,
the push range at push time), reports verified secrets only, and fails closed on
a finding.

Deliberately **out of scope**:

- No `ci: skip:` block. That is prescribed for the hosted pre-commit.ci sandbox,
  which has no network access. No Triton repo uses pre-commit.ci — CI runs
  pre-commit from `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` — so it would be dead config.
- No `default_install_hook_types` change. Activation is a developer action;
  changing that key would alter install behaviour for *every* hook in the repo,
  not just this one. Tracked separately.

## Changes

- Add `NVIDIA/security-workflows` `secret-scan-trufflehog` @ `v0.3.0` as the
  first entry under `repos:`.

## Affected Files

- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`

## Test plan

- `pre-commit validate-config` — passes.
- `pre-commit run secret-scan-trufflehog --all-files` — passes, with **zero**
  pre-existing verified secrets, so CI does not break on merge.
- TruffleHog **3.95.9** confirmed installed into pre-commit's Python environment
  and executed, so the hook is functional rather than a silent no-op.
- Blast radius is bounded: `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` runs
  `pre-commit run --files` against PR-modified paths only, never `--all-files`.

## Caveats

Editing the config alone scans nothing. Each contributor must run once per clone:

```
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push
```

Without the second, the `pre-push` stage stays dormant.

body:
## Summary

Removes `llvm/test/Transforms/OpenMP/DELETE_NOTE_remove_spmdization_guarding.md`, a scratch triage note that was accidentally committed by 58cb585ca021 (#3884) alongside the three deviceRTL test deletions that PR was meant to make.

The note was never intended to land. It is also stale and self-contradictory: it describes the test removal as pending approval ("do not proceed with removal until confirmation") in the very commit that performed the removal. A lit test directory is not the right place to record a triage decision either.

No functional change. The file has no build or test consumer.

## Rationale for the original test removal

The commit message on #3884 was garbled during authoring (literal `\n` sequences and a block of accidentally interpolated binary output), so the reasoning for deleting those tests is restated here and in this PR's commit message:

- `custom_state_machines.ll`, `spmdization.ll` and `spmdization_guarding.ll` were ROCm copies of tests for the old CUDA-derived `deviceRTLs/common` device runtime. That runtime was replaced by the current C++ implementation and the tests were removed upstream.
- Equivalent coverage exists upstream in the newer format, so the ROCm copies were duplicated and stale, and caused merge conflicts.
- Validated against the srock toolchain before removal: two of the three passed, and `spmdization_guarding.ll` differed only cosmetically (addrspace/select form and attribute renumbering), with no change in runtime semantics.

## Test plan

- Deletes a `.md` file only; no code, build rule, or lit test references it.
- `rg 'DELETE_NOTE'` across the tree returns no other hits.

body:
## What changed

- add `Jido.Connect.prepare/4` and `commit/4` with an expiring, secret-free execution snapshot
- revalidate action, input, connection, credential lease, host binding, execution ID, and idempotency key before commit
- require host-issued authorization evidence for confirmation policies; boolean confirmation is rejected
- keep direct mutation calls as a named compatibility mode and let strict hosts deny them
- resolve MCP endpoints from the selected Jido Connect connection and short-lived credential lease
- use tenant- and connection-specific string IDs so same-name MCP connections do not share clients or credentials
- replace an endpoint safely when its credential material rotates
- return stable MCP tool schema hashes and reject schema drift before a mutating tool call
- use the ExMCP-backed `jido_mcp` `main` branch during repository development while keeping the Hex release dependency for package tasks

## Why

Persistent, multi-persona hosts must select one exact connection before approval and keep that binding through execution. They also need more than one MCP connection for the same provider, such as two Slack identities, without global endpoint or credential crossover.

The core remains storage-free. Hosts own personas, connection persistence, secrets, approval records, replay claims, and audit data.

## Compatibility

Reads continue to use direct invocation. Direct calls that require confirmation remain available by default with a deprecation warning. Strict hosts can set `config :jido_connect, direct_mutation_mode: :deny`.

## Validation

- `mix compile --warnings-as-errors`

author: yushuqin
body:
## Description

During Reshard `SwitchWrites`, `stream_migrator` reads all VReplication streams on source shards. OnlineDDL migrations that have already completed (or failed/cancelled) leave behind Stopped VReplication streams that linger until `gcArtifacts()` cleans them up (~24h later). These dead streams cause a spurious "cannot migrate until all streams are running" error, blocking `SwitchWrites`.

This PR cross-references `_vt.schema_migrations.migration_status` for any `WorkflowType=OnlineDDL` stream. If the migration has reached a terminal state (`complete`, `failed`, or `cancelled`), the stream is filtered out — matching the same criteria used by `gcArtifacts()` in the OnlineDDL executor.

Both the legacy (VReplicationExec/SQL) and gRPC (ReadVReplicationWorkflows) code paths are covered.

## Related Issue(s)

Fixes a production issue where Reshard SwitchWrites is blocked by dead OnlineDDL VReplication streams.

## Checklist

- [ ] "Backport to:" labels have been added if this change should be back-ported to release branches
- [ ] If this change is to be back-ported to previous releases, a justification is included in the PR description
- [ ] Tests were added or are not required
- [ ] Did the new or modified tests pass consistently locally and on CI?
- [x] Documentation was added or is not required

## Deployment Notes

No migrations or configuration changes needed. The filtering is transparent — terminal OnlineDDL streams that were previously blocking SwitchWrites will now be silently skipped.

### AI Disclosure

This PR was written primarily by Claude Code with direction and review from the author.

author: mc-nv
body:
## Description

Enables the NVIDIA `secret-scan-trufflehog` pre-commit hook, pinned to `v0.3.0`,
as the first entry under `repos:` so scanning runs before any formatter rewrites
the working tree.

This adopts the centrally maintained hook published by `NVIDIA/security-workflows`
rather than a hand-rolled TruffleHog invocation, so the scanner version and its
per-platform checksums are bumped in one reviewed place instead of 27.

`v0.3.0` is pinned deliberately. It installs the scanner inside pre-commit's own
Python environment — removing the shell installer, so Windows works without Git
Bash — and it adds `--exclude-detectors=lob`. That exclusion matters here: a Lob
API key is `test_` followed by 35 characters, so the detector matches ordinary
pytest function names such as `test_gpu_conf_compute_attestation_report`, and
Lob's verifier reports them as *verified* — the one result class this hook fails
on.

Behaviour: scans only the files pre-commit supplies (staged files at commit time,
the push range at push time), reports verified secrets only, and fails closed on
a finding.

Deliberately **out of scope**:

- No `ci: skip:` block. That is prescribed for the hosted pre-commit.ci sandbox,
  which has no network access. No Triton repo uses pre-commit.ci — CI runs
  pre-commit from `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` — so it would be dead config.
- No `default_install_hook_types` change. Activation is a developer action;
  changing that key would alter install behaviour for *every* hook in the repo,
  not just this one. Tracked separately.

## Changes

- Add `NVIDIA/security-workflows` `secret-scan-trufflehog` @ `v0.3.0` as the
  first entry under `repos:`.

## Affected Files

- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`

## Test plan

- `pre-commit validate-config` — passes.
- `pre-commit run secret-scan-trufflehog --all-files` — passes, with **zero**
  pre-existing verified secrets, so CI does not break on merge.
- TruffleHog **3.95.9** confirmed installed into pre-commit's Python environment
  and executed, so the hook is functional rather than a silent no-op.
- Blast radius is bounded: `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` runs
  `pre-commit run --files` against PR-modified paths only, never `--all-files`.

## Caveats

Editing the config alone scans nothing. Each contributor must run once per clone:

```
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push
```

Without the second, the `pre-push` stage stays dormant.

author: ai-sdk-factory[bot]
body:
## Background

Resumed @ai-sdk/harness-opencode sessions could silently return the previous turn's assistant response as a successful reply when the event stream closed prematurely.

## Root Cause

Stream completion resolved the current turn's settlement promise, after which the fallback selected the newest persisted assistant message without a current-turn fence. The reproduction confirmed this by emitting the prior assistant text with a synthetic successful finish-step.

## Summary

Distinguished event settlement from premature stream closure, fenced fallback snapshots against the pre-prompt assistant, and made interrupted or uncorrelated turns fail instead of synthesizing success. Added a patch changeset.

## Testing

Added unit coverage verifying that fallback rejects the baseline assistant, accepts a newer assistant, and fails closed when the baseline lacks a usable ID.

## End-to-end Validation

- `pnpm -C examples/ai-functions exec tsx src/reproduction/harness-opencode-cold-resume-stale-reply.ts` — exited 1 with the exact reproduction signal before the fix; exited 0 afterward and confirmed rejection without stale output.

## Related Issues

Fixes #18933

Closes #18935

author: liamthura
body:
Stacked on #77, like #79 — GitHub retargets to `main` when that merges.

You asked for a factual audit of the docs after the quick-start turned out to be a day stale. I checked all 21 pages against the code, the schema and the running instance. **Three claims were wrong.**

## 1. `capture.mdx` overstated observation protection

> "the newest 50 are kept, and rows you have never looked at are protected from being trimmed"

`proposals_store.py:19-21` — `NOTE_WINDOW = 50`, but `NOTE_BACKSTOP = 100`, and the code's own comment says unseen rows "are protected **only up to here**". Past 100 pending notes, `_evict()` drops the `seen_at is not null` filter and takes them too.

"The newest 50" was also not the eviction order. Victims are `order by (seen_at is null), seen_count asc, created_at asc` — opened rows first, least-opened, then oldest. An old unopened observation outlives a newer opened one.

## 2. `editor.mdx` named a button that doesn't exist

> "a **Save changes** button appears instead"

It's **"Save now"** (`Header.jsx:88`). The app's own settings panel already said so (`AccountPanel.jsx:214`: *"a Save now button instead"*), so the docs were the only place with the wrong name.

## 3. `database.mdx` listed 6 tables; there are 17

`public` was missing **`persona_proposals`** — the entire review queue `capture.mdx` is about — and `waitlist`. And there's a whole **`better_auth` schema** with nine more that no page mentioned.

Per your call, `invite_codes` is left out. It's already named in `self-hosting.mdx`'s `INVITE_ONLY` row, so nothing is lost.

## One error of my own

My first draft credited migration `0003` with all nine `better_auth` tables. It creates the five sign-in ones; `0006` adds the four OAuth ones. Corrected before pushing.

## What held up

| Checked | Result |
|---|---|
| 8 MCP tool names across 8 pages | all registered, none retired |
| 21 env vars / constants | all present in code |
| Repo paths, HTTP endpoints | all resolve |
| 10 sections: keys, titles, `core` flags, opt-in defaults | match the manifests exactly |
| Scope→section matrix in `reading.mdx` | matches `scope_contributions`, including `aesthetics` under `minimal` |
| Numeric claims | link cap 10 · limit 1–25 default 10 · `get_entity` 25 · staleness 30d · `EMBEDDING_DIM` 1024 · password 8 · access token `10 * 60` · `seen N×` |
| Python 3.11 in production, both Dockerfiles, the build-context warning | correct |
| "Alembic owns Better Auth's tables" | correct |

Two I'd have got wrong by assuming: `preferences` declares **no** `scope_contributions` yet reaches every scope (`sections.py:36 ALWAYS_ON`, already explained at `pack-reference.mdx:66`), and the eleventh pack directory is `_template` with `"key": "example"` inside, skipped by `pack_loader.py:448` — so "ten sections" is right.

## Verification

`next build` + `check:links`: 363 links, 469 anchors, all resolve.

author: mahiatlinux
body:
An Ubuntu user reports Unsloth Desktop freezing and then dying with the machine.

`--fit on` places what it can in VRAM and spills the rest into host memory with
no ceiling of its own, and nothing upstream of llama-server prices that spill.
The weights are memory-mapped, so an oversized remainder does not fail an
allocation: the kernel evicts and re-reads the mapping every token until the
machine stops responding, and systemd-oomd then kills the whole app slice.

The reported session loaded a 13.3 GB `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat` GGUF plus a
1.1 GB mmproj and a 1.8 GB KV cache onto a card with 4877 MiB free, leaving
about 11 GB to run from system RAM. The server log ends mid-poll with no
shutdown line and no `parent_watchdog.parent_exited`, which is what a SIGKILL of
the whole process group looks like.

`llama_cpp.py` already refuses this on Apple unified memory
(`_apple_metal_memory_budget_bytes`) and on AMD APUs
(`_apu_ram_shortfall_message`), but `_amd_apu_wants_unified_memory` is false for
a discrete card, so CUDA and ROCm hosts had no guard at all.

## What it checks

```
refuse when  model_bytes - free_vram  >  available_ram - 2 GiB
```

Weights only, against the whole free VRAM pool, read from the finished argv so
the model path is the one the child opens. That is a strict lower bound on what
the launch must hold: the KV cache, projector, drafter and compute buffers all
add to residency, and a layer or device pin only narrows the VRAM actually
reachable.

Every term left out therefore moves the estimate down, never up, so no missing
term can turn an allowed load into a refused one. The guard models no placement
at all, which is what keeps it from having to track llama.cpp's placement
surface flag by flag. It abstains on an unsized model, an unprobed GPU pool, or
unknown available RAM.

Two signals take no VRAM credit on their own: the ROCm arch gate finding no
kernels for any card present, and a paravirtual Metal launch. Each names a device
that was seen and ruled out, so the empty pool beside it is the gate's own doing.
A launch masked off every device and a build shipping no GPU backend also take no
credit, but only where a pool was actually probed: neither says a device exists,
so on an empty pool they cannot separate a GPU-less host from a probe that threw.
An RPC launch abstains outright, since it places layers on remote devices this
cannot size.

`UNSLOTH_ALLOW_HOST_OFFLOAD=1` abstains, and the refusal names it, so a user who
accepts the paging can still load a variant the picker offers. Same shape as
`UNSLOTH_ALLOW_PARAVIRTUAL_METAL`, the file's existing escape for a hard guard.

The guard reads the finished argv, so it cannot answer until after the route has
taken `acquire_for(CHAT)`, evicted a resident Images/Video pipeline and cancelled
the running generations. `host_offload_refusal_for_intent` asks the same function
ahead of that handoff, crediting the ungated probe that every narrowing the launch
applies only shrinks, so it refuses a strict subset and fails open into the launch
copy. Same placement and same reason as `non_chat_gguf_refusal_for_intent`.

An earlier revision of this PR modelled the placement in full and was rewritten;
`2220d79de` and the comment above it record why.

## Testing

`test_host_offload_ram_guard.py` covers the arithmetic. The placement suite
drives `load_model` end to end: the field case refuses, the same load on a large
RAM host launches, free VRAM offsets the charge, and each abstention holds. A
parametrised case asserts the floor property directly, that `-ngl 0`, `--mlock`,
`--no-mmap`, `--device none` and `--no-kv-offload` each move bytes onto the host
or narrow reachable VRAM and so can never produce a refusal the floor would not
already reach.

Every fix in this PR carries a regression test verified to fail against the code
before it, and each of the two probed-pool gates is pinned by its own arm: gating
only the build probe fails the zero-offload case, gating only zero-offload fails
the CPU-only-build case. 366 tests pass across the guard, placement, paravirtual,
arch-gate and preflight suites, 184 across the route suites, and the wide-sweep
failure set is identical to a clean tree.

Also run end to end against the real `llama-server` (`b10360`, Darwin arm64) with
a real GGUF, simulating only free VRAM and `MemAvailable`. Each cell is a real
spawn, health wait and HTTP completion: a shortfall refuses and names the escape,
the escape starts the server and serves, an empty pool with a CPU-only build and
an empty pool with manual zero-offload both abstain and serve, and a probed pool
with a CPU-only build still refuses. A separate cell reproduces the Apple Silicon
false refusal with nothing about the GPU simulated, real `_get_gpu_memory()`
returning `[]`: refused before this change, served after.

author: mc-nv
body:
## Description

Enables the NVIDIA `secret-scan-trufflehog` pre-commit hook, pinned to `v0.3.0`,
as the first entry under `repos:` so scanning runs before any formatter rewrites
the working tree.

This adopts the centrally maintained hook published by `NVIDIA/security-workflows`
rather than a hand-rolled TruffleHog invocation, so the scanner version and its
per-platform checksums are bumped in one reviewed place instead of 27.

`v0.3.0` is pinned deliberately. It installs the scanner inside pre-commit's own
Python environment — removing the shell installer, so Windows works without Git
Bash — and it adds `--exclude-detectors=lob`. That exclusion matters here: a Lob
API key is `test_` followed by 35 characters, so the detector matches ordinary
pytest function names such as `test_gpu_conf_compute_attestation_report`, and
Lob's verifier reports them as *verified* — the one result class this hook fails
on.

Behaviour: scans only the files pre-commit supplies (staged files at commit time,
the push range at push time), reports verified secrets only, and fails closed on
a finding.

Deliberately **out of scope**:

- No `ci: skip:` block. That is prescribed for the hosted pre-commit.ci sandbox,
  which has no network access. No Triton repo uses pre-commit.ci — CI runs
  pre-commit from `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` — so it would be dead config.
- No `default_install_hook_types` change. Activation is a developer action;
  changing that key would alter install behaviour for *every* hook in the repo,
  not just this one. Tracked separately.

## Changes

- Add `NVIDIA/security-workflows` `secret-scan-trufflehog` @ `v0.3.0` as the
  first entry under `repos:`.

## Affected Files

- `.pre-commit-config.yaml`

## Test plan

- `pre-commit validate-config` — passes.
- `pre-commit run secret-scan-trufflehog --all-files` — passes, with **zero**
  pre-existing verified secrets, so CI does not break on merge.
- TruffleHog **3.95.9** confirmed installed into pre-commit's Python environment
  and executed, so the hook is functional rather than a silent no-op.
- Blast radius is bounded: `.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml` runs
  `pre-commit run --files` against PR-modified paths only, never `--all-files`.

## Caveats

Editing the config alone scans nothing. Each contributor must run once per clone:

```
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-commit
pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push
```

Without the second, the `pre-push` stage stays dormant.

author: connectsudhindra-gif
body:
## Summary

Part of #2442 (streaming LLM instrumentation): "Cost tracking should accumulate as chunks arrive (not just at end)". **Stacked on #2690** (sync OpenAI streaming; that commit and #2689's are included in the diff until they merge).

### The bug

`OpenAICallback.handle_generation_chunk` hard-codes `token_usage={}` on the `finish_reason == "stop"` chunk. Confirmed live against a real server: prompt/completion tokens were **always 0** for a streamed OpenAI call before this fix, even when the caller passed `stream_options={"include_usage": True}` -- **27/4 after** the fix, for the same request.

Root cause: OpenAI only sends real usage on a *separate* trailing chunk with empty `choices` (and only when `include_usage` is requested) -- sent right after, not on, the `"stop"` chunk. The existing code finalized the whole generation record the moment it saw `finish_reason == "stop"`, before that trailing chunk ever arrived, so the real numbers were never looked at. Non-streaming responses were unaffected; this was streaming-only.

### The fix

- `handle_generation_chunk` no longer finalizes on `"stop"` -- it just accumulates text, and stashes real usage from whichever chunk carries it (if any).
- A new `finalize_stream()` flushes whatever was accumulated into a real cost record -- real usage if it arrived, empty otherwise (same fallback as before, so behavior for callers who don't request `include_usage` is unchanged).
- The existing stream-iterator wrapping in `_handle_response` now calls `finalize_stream()` via `on_done`, once, when the stream is *actually* exhausted -- matching how a stream really ends, instead of guessing from a single chunk's shape.
- Also extended the per-span streaming-attributes helper from #2690 to write real `COST.NUM_PROMPT_TOKENS`/`NUM_COMPLETION_TOKENS`/`NUM_TOKENS` onto the span once known (previously stuck at whatever the synchronous, pre-consumption `COST.*` dict had -- i.e. zero -- for every streamed call), alongside the `CHUNKS_RECEIVED`/`TOKENS_PER_SECOND` it already recorded. Same graceful no-op if the span has already closed by the time the stream finishes.

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/unit/providers/test_openai_streaming_cost_accumulation.py` (4 new tests): real usage from a trailing chunk gets picked up correctly; the no-`include_usage` case still records the request (just with $0 cost, not silently dropped); `finalize_stream()` on nothing accumulated is a no-op; a full `OpenAICostComputer`-style end-to-end path produces real, non-zero cost for a known-priced model (`gpt-4o-mini`).
- [x] Fixed an under-specified `Mock` in the existing `test_openai_streaming_span_attributes.py` that this change's stricter usage handling exposed (a `Mock(completion_tokens=7)` with no other fields set was silently returning more mocks for `prompt_tokens`/`total_tokens` instead of the real ints a live OpenAI response always has) -- now asserts the new `COST.NUM_*` span attributes too.
- [x] Verified live against a real server end-to-end: prompt/completion tokens correctly non-zero after the fix, using a real streamed request with `stream_options={"include_usage": True}`.
- [x] Existing `test_otel_instrument.py`, `test_tru_llama_workflow.py`, `test_openai_capabilities.py`, `test_async_openai_capabilities.py` all still pass -- no regression to non-streaming cost tracking or anything else sharing this callback class.
- [x] `ruff check` / `ruff format --check` (pinned `0.5.5`) pass.

author: brcampidelli
body:
> Based on #78 — GitHub will retarget this to `main` when that merges.

`chimera redteam` measures one run: content arrives untrusted, the harmful call is refused, and the whole picture ends with the process. Persistent memory is the other shape, and nothing measured it:

```
run A   reads a poisoned page, writes what it "learned" to memory
run B   asks an unrelated question days later, recall hands the planted fact to the model
```

Three layers already sat between those two runs and none had a number under it: the `tainted` provenance flag, the recall admission gate, and the `[unverified]` label the fact wears into the prompt. `chimera memory-poison` ablates them — offline, deterministic, no key, nothing leaves the machine.

**The headline is what arrives UNMARKED, not what is blocked.** A poisoned fact carrying its origin is one the model was warned about; an unlabelled one is indistinguishable from something the agent verified itself. A single "the defense works" number would have been compatible with any one layer doing nothing at all, which is why this is an ablation.

## The first measurement

| configuration | poison recalled | **poison unmarked** | **honest memory lost** | gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `all` (shipped) | 43% | **0%** | **25%** | **FAIL** |
| `no_taint` | 43% | 43% | 25% | FAIL |
| `no_gate` | 100% | **0%** | **0%** | **pass** |
| `no_label` | 43% | 43% | 25% | FAIL |
| `none` | 100% | 100% | 0% | FAIL |

Two of these do not flatter us, and both are pinned as tests so that changing the answer is a deliberate act.

**The shipped configuration fails its own gate — on cost, not on protection.** It marks 100% of the poison and destroys a quarter of honest memory doing it. The casualties are named: a security document that quotes an attack in order to explain it, and a support ticket forwarding an attempt. A pattern matcher on content cannot tell a quote from a command, and a repository whose own documentation discusses prompt injection will keep producing them.

**On this corpus the content gate contributes nothing the provenance label does not already cover.** `no_gate` and `all` report the *same* 0% unmarked; every poison row the gate blocks is one the label already marks. Its entire measured effect here is the honest memory it removes. Fifteen hand-authored rows is a pointer and **not** a verdict — nothing has been deleted on the strength of it, and the preregistration says that explicitly along with the readings it does not license.

The third reading is the one that justifies provenance existing: `quiet_false_fact`, `quiet_wrong_endpoint` and `exfil_habit` carry no override marker and read exactly like a fact learned from a docs page, because that is the shape they were written in. No pattern matcher separates them from truth. Only the origin travels with them — now with a number under it instead of a design note.

## The corpus change, recorded rather than made quietly

The benign arm first returned **0% loss under every configuration** — a control that never fires, which says nothing about a defense's cost. Two realistic rows were added *before* that corpus was read, and the change is written into `bench/memory_poison/PREREGISTRATION.md`. The thresholds were fixed first and were not touched.

## The apparatus is tested harder than the results

This is the file that could most easily lie, and `bench/injection` already walked into that once — a number that was an artifact of the harness and got read as a property of the defense. So there are tests that run B genuinely reads from disk rather than the writer's state; that every payload is reachable with the defenses off (or the bench would be measuring recall blind spots and flattering every arm equally); that a poison nobody asks for is not scored as protected; and that refusing everything does not pass the gate.

Both mutations tried against it — always-labelled, and gate-never-applied — are caught by two or more tests.

---

**Verification.** Full suite in WSL: ruff clean, mypy `--strict` reports nothing in any changed file, 2948 passed. The 18 failures are pre-existing environment breakage in this WSL venv, 12 confirmed failing on unmodified `main`.

One thing found on the way and worth a separate look: `_cli_snapshot.json` records `generated_for` from the *installed* dist metadata rather than the repo version, so regenerating it in an environment with a stale editable install silently downgrades the field. It did exactly that here and was caught before pushing.

author: olivertransf
body:
## Summary

This is the accumulated hub work on `feat/hub-ui-multiguessr` (58 commits ahead of `main`). It restyles the product around a shared grey-black system, removes the old GeoHub chrome that fought that system, then fixes MultiGuessr and maps browse so those surfaces actually play.

Uncommitted friends/spectate work is **not** in this PR.

### Design system and chrome

- Shared tokens: page background `#0c0d0f`, cards `#1c1e22`, accent `#2f7fff`.
- Replaces navy card surfaces and the old site navbar. Home, play, maps, profile, duel/streak/multi create, and result/leaderboard chrome use the same card language.
- Home is a single scrolling page: play tiles, featured world maps, continue list, friends rail. No Play/Maps/Friends tab bar.
- Map photos are gone from hub lists. Identity is flag emoji or letter tiles (`MapRowTile`).
- Profile is rebuilt as home-card chrome (identity + stats), not the old banner layout.
- Hero copy is itsturkey, with more vertical space.

### Play, maps, and create flows

- Map play is a two-column card: settings/filters on one side, start actions on the other. Visual-restriction chips stretch in that column.
- Duel, streak, and MultiGuessr create lobbies match that map-play layout (same picker, same settings stack, `PageBackLink`).
- Map picker is compact rows with search. Country maps show flags.
- `/maps` browse is compact 3-column rows (2 on tablet, 1 on phone). Countries tab has a local search by name or ISO code (`filterCountryMapsByQuery`). Country rows show flags. This is not the global site `Searchbar`.

### Continue games

- Ongoing/continue list sorts by last used (`lastUsedAt` from game, live view, or guess-map activity).
- Hide is persisted and survives refetch. Hidden games do not come back on reload. Toast undo shows two games when relevant.

### MultiGuessr

- Street View bootstraps Maps itself. It does not wait on GuessMap `onGoogleApiLoaded`. Loading stays inside the pano. No `LoadingPage` overlay per panel (those stacked and hung the grid).
- One interactive guess map on the **active** playable panel. Click another playable panel to focus it.
- GuessMap is not torn down just because a panel is inactive or in cooldown. Unmounting after Maps was already warm left the next panel unable to place a pin. After a panel has been focused, the map stays mounted and is hidden with `visibility` / `pointer-events`. Pins use GoogleMapReact `onClick` as well as `map.click`.
- Default World in MultiGuessr uses `getHomeDefaultWorldMapId()` from `NEXT_PUBLIC_HOME_MAP_CARDS` (name starting with `Default World`). The leftover GeoHub world id `6185df7a…` is a tiny stub and repeated the same pano. `getLocations` remaps that legacy id. Country-streak sampling still uses official-world pins. Picker no longer relabels the stub as Default World.

### Maps loader

- `googleMapLoaderAsync` uses `loading=async` and waits for `importLibrary('core'|'maps'|'streetView')` so `LatLng` / `Map` are constructors. GuessMap still owns the guess-map instance. Do not seed `googleMapsConfig` with `map: null`.
- Result markers wait until guesses have coordinates. `setCenter` waits until a real guess map exists.

### Country tips

- Plonk It guides, `PlonkitGuideLauncher`, `/api/plonkit-guide`, and geotips overlays are removed from Street View, play settings, results, streaks, and duels. Duel recap `plonkMapLabel` is the map name chip, not tips.

### Build

- `DAILY_CHALLENGE_DETAILS` now includes `_id: DAILY_CHALLENGE_ID` so analytics and ongoing typecheck (`ListItem` was failing Vercel).
- Maps `importLibrary` results are treated as objects when copying constructors onto `google.maps`.

## Test plan

- [ ] `yarn tsc --noEmit` and Vercel `yarn run build` succeed
- [ ] Home, map play, duel/streak/multi create, profile, and leaderboards use grey-black cards on `#0c0d0f`
- [ ] No site navbar; home scrolls as one page
- [ ] Continue list sorts by last used; hide persists across refresh; undo works
- [ ] MultiGuessr Default World gives different locations each round (not the leftover GeoHub world)
- [ ] After guessing on panel 1, panel 2 accepts a pin without a refresh
- [ ] Street View loads on MultiGuessr without full-screen stacked spinners
- [ ] `/maps` Countries: flags, compact rows, search by “France” or `fr`
- [ ] Normal World game still loads Street View and can place a guess-map pin
- [ ] Daily challenge and ongoing tiles still resolve a map id
- [ ] No Plonk It / country-tips UI in play or results

author: gutierrezje
body:
## What changed

`VISION.md` now names DiffOwl as a local verification layer built from three shared capabilities: impact context, a claim ledger, and independent verification.

The roadmap is deliberately shape-first:

1. Define the smallest module-impact slice.
2. Ship the TypeScript index with deterministic graph tests.
3. Run a small number of targeted reviewer comparisons after the new context exists.
4. Define incremental-review invalidation.
5. Add coalesced warming or an opt-in checker when the workflow calls for it.

The document also:

- calls the first graph slice a module-impact index rather than a full call graph;
- keeps the disposable index lifecycle separate from durable finding state without prescribing separate databases;
- makes checker publication policy user-controlled while preserving one canonical review;
- treats edge precision/recall and context latency as module diagnostics, with useful findings as the product outcome;
- distinguishes offline corpus evals from lightweight, local disposition analytics;
- treats `dismissed / created` as a smoke alarm rather than a quality score;
- defers vectors, remote telemetry, language breadth, and multi-model ensembles.

## Why

The product bet was spread across conversation, and the old roadmap overclaimed both the graph and delta-aware review. It also risked making eval expansion the next milestone before DiffOwl had the intended context shape.

The revised vision freezes the product thesis while leaving implementation details to the graph-slice design.

## How it was verified

- Read against the current shipped implementation: reference context still uses `git grep`; findings classify repeated observations without skipping the model.
- Reviewed the final documentation diff for internal contradictions.
- `git diff --check` passes.
- Only `VISION.md` changed.

## Intentionally out of scope

No graph implementation, invalidation code, checker mode, analytics command, OLAP system, telemetry, or eval-corpus expansion. Discoverability work remains a separate, small parallel track.

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Low Risk**
> Documentation-only change to product vision and roadmap; no runtime, security, or data-handling code.
> 
> **Overview**
> **`VISION.md`** is updated to state the product thesis explicitly: one review combines **impact context**, a **claim ledger**, and **independent verification**, with a single canonical output and a disposable module-impact index kept separate from durable finding state.
> 
> The roadmap is reshaped to be **shape-first**: next milestone is a small **TypeScript module-impact index** behind one context-building interface (with deterministic graph tests), then targeted harness comparisons, then **incremental-review invalidation** and optional warming—not growing the eval corpus or implying delta-aware branch review skips the model today.
> 
> The doc also **tightens claims** shipped vs future work: fingerprint classification on repeat branch reviews is not incremental review; eval harness is supporting evidence; vectors, multi-model ensembles, remote telemetry, and per-commit hooks as incremental design are deferred. It adds **local disposition analytics** guidance, renames the graph slice honestly, and refreshes **near-term decision** and **non-goals** to match.

author: magnus-encoded
body:
One slice of #164 — **not** the whole issue. Specifically: the actions that were *absent* rather than merely unlabelled.

## What was actually broken

A flick and a pinch are the whole of how this app changes **Resolution**. Both screen readers claim those gestures for their own navigation. So for a TalkBack or VoiceOver user:

- **The contact light** (#145) — `toggleContactLight` had exactly one call site in the entire app, the swipe-right handler.
- **The other timelines** — `setZoomedOut` had one user-facing call site, the pinch. (The other is a `LaunchedEffect` after a card swap.)

Not "hard to reach". No route in at all. Two features that don't exist for a blind user, on both platforms.

Verified by call-site audit rather than assumed — the top bar's Person icon calls `onOpenConnect`, which is a *different* target from the swipe's `onOpenNearby`, so I checked each one rather than trusting that a visible button covered it.

## The one I owe

`GigView`'s "Make a Spotify playlist" was a **button** until iteration one of this session moved it to swipe-left for grammar consistency (#181, PR #184). The button was reachable; the gesture is not. That change quietly took the action away from a reader, and this puts it back as an accessibility action — which is what the grammar should have cost: nothing.

## The fix

The gestures are untouched. These are the same calls from another door — `customActions` on Android's timeline, `.accessibilityAction` on iOS's. Also `.accessibilityAction(.escape)` for the iOS back-swipe, and a label on the back chevron, which unlabelled reads as *"chevron left"* — a shape, where every other control here is named by what it does.

Labels are verbs, and the toggles say **which way they go** ("Turn the contact light off" vs "on"), because both readers announce these out of context with nothing on screen to disambiguate them.

## Testing, and its limits

Compile only. **No screen-reader pass has been run** — #164 asks for one on each platform and I can't do it from here. Custom actions are the kind of thing that compiles clean and still lands wrong (wrong element, unhelpful label, wrong order in the rotor), so this wants a real TalkBack/VoiceOver pass before anyone considers that checklist line done.

## Still open on #164

Everything else, which is most of it: the audit of every element, reading order, the custom-drawn spine (a `Canvas` that conveys the entire structure of the Line and currently exposes nothing), dynamic announcements, touch targets, contrast, and the manual passes. iOS in particular still has **near-zero** accessibility annotation outside this change.

That issue is a programme of work, not a task — worth splitting per surface if it's going to be worked AFK.

author: nghaiz
body:
`develop` is red and PR #56 could not go green. Neither is caused by the change under review — this is the cause, and it is pre-existing.

## The failure

`build-test (ubuntu-latest)` ran for **15m15s** and was cancelled by the job timeout, twice in a row on the same commit. No test was reported as failing, because none did — one hung.

Attribution was the expensive part. `dotnet test` on the solution interleaves five assemblies' console output, so the last line printed named an unrelated test that had passed. Counting completed tests per assembly is what found it:

| Assembly | Completed | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `Protocol.Tests` | 198 | 198 |
| `Replication.Tests` | 422 | 422 |
| `Transport.Tests` | 85 | 85 |
| `Configuration.Tests` | 32 | 32 |
| **`MasterServer.Tests`** | **75** | **77** |

The two missing names were `MasterClientPollTests.ResponseCompletesOnlyWhenPollRuns` and `.ErrorPushCompletesPendingRequestDuringPoll`.

## Why they hang

Both write a frame onto a loopback socket, `await Task.Delay(20)`, call `Poll()` once, then `await request` **with no timeout**.

The 20 ms delay is a bet that the write has been read into the client's queue by the time `Poll()` runs. A loaded runner loses that bet: `Poll()` finds nothing, the request stays pending, and the await blocks forever. The job burns its whole budget and dies without naming a culprit.

## The fix

A longer delay is the same bet at higher stakes. `PollUntil` calls `Poll()` until the request settles or ten seconds pass, then throws a `TimeoutException` saying what never arrived. The socket awaits (`accept`, `connect`, frame read/write) are bounded the same way.

`PollUntil` is **synchronous deliberately**. The assertion right after it compares the caller's thread id against the one the completing `Poll()` ran on — that comparison *is* the Poll() contract, the thing that keeps Unity API use on the main thread. An `await` inside the pump would let the test resume on a different pool thread and turn that assertion into a comparison of two unrelated numbers that passes or fails by luck.

The `Assert.False(request.IsCompleted)` check before the pump is kept: it fails only in the safe direction, since a slow runner means the response has not arrived either.

## Still outstanding, not fixed here

`develop`'s post-merge run of #55 failed differently — on **windows**, with a real fast failure in `Ironfront.Net.Transport.Tests.ControlAndSocketTests.TransportStatsExposeRatesAndDiagnosticsAfterAWindow`. Same code passed on that PR's own run, so it is a second, independent flake, in Dev B's rate-window test. It fails in two seconds rather than fifteen minutes, so it is not blocking, and it is not mine to guess at. Flagged rather than touched.

## Verification

- Both tests: **117 ms**, passing
- `dotnet test Ironfront.sln -c Release` — **814 passed, 0 failed**
- `dotnet format style` / `analyzers --verify-no-changes` — clean

author: huntharo
body:
Stacked on #1647 — review that first; this PR's diff is against its branch.

## Why

The explorer measures one of the two things that drive replay cost, and renders all of it as numerals. Every quantity is a number in the same size, weight, and color, so ranking thirteen cases means reading thirteen numbers.

The missing driver is **round trips**. A turn that returns one enormous result is a filtering problem; a turn that makes sixty small calls is a round-trip problem, because each trip replays the whole accumulated context. The data to show it (`turnId`, `observedAt` on every invocation) was already persisted — nothing here adds IPC or contract fields.

## What changed

**Turn strip.** One row per turn over *every* accounted call, not just flagged ones — quiet calls replay context exactly like loud ones. Solid bar = output tokens, tick rail = round trips, deliberately different marks because they are different problems. Click to filter the case list.

**Summary band.** Leads with tokens rather than characters, against a real denominator (flagged share of all accounted tool output). The composition bar answers "where did it go" in a 5px strip and doubles as the category filter, replacing the raw-enum `<select>`. It steps one accent down in strength rather than spending the product's whole color budget on a five-color legend.

**Ranked cases with cap meters.** Sorted largest-first, measured against the observed model-visible output cap the analyzer already reasons about — an absolute denominator, so a pinned bar means "the harness will truncate this." That constant moved to `packages/shared` so the meter and the detector that flagged the case cannot drift apart; the analyzer keeps its local names and imports the values.

**Row labels elided in the middle.** Shell invocations in one turn routinely share a 60-character prefix, and head-truncation rendered several rows byte-identical. The distinguishing tail now survives; the CSS end-ellipsis that would undo it is deliberately absent (commented, so it doesn't get "fixed" back).

**Detail pane collapsed to decisions.** Identity on one line with expand, facts as compact pills instead of a seven-row `<dl>`, steering behind a disclosure. The command appeared three times on screen; now once. The budget card states the replay math concretely: *"17,771 chars · replayed on the 57 later round trips in this turn."*

**Style-guide fixes.** Button hierarchy (primary/secondary/ghost) instead of one blanket `.incident-explorer button` selector; Close dropped (duplicated the OS control); a completed analysis no longer renders in warning amber; `aria-current` / `aria-pressed` on selection and filters, which previously had no accessible state at all.

## Verification

- `pnpm typecheck`, `lint:eslint` (0 errors), `lint:colors`, `lint:boundaries` all pass.
- 27 tests across the window and a new pure-derivation module; the 8 pre-existing window tests pass unmodified.
- Rendered against the real `app.css` in a browser to check the result rather than assume it — that pass is what caught the end-ellipsis undoing the middle-elision, and a turn-strip "critical" flag that was true for every row.
- Full `pnpm test`: 4 files / 12 failures, all in `desktop-main` files untouched here (`acp-backend-adapter`, `app-server-ipc`, `backend-registry`, `codex-environment-runtime`). **Confirmed pre-existing** — the same files fail identically on the unmodified base branch, and each passes in isolation.

author: oc2co
body:
## Problem

**Console-flash regression:** commit d3d621f7c (June 2026, "revert(windows): roll back terminal-popup PRs #53791 #53810 #53829") bulk-reverted three earlier windows-hide-flag fixes across ~40 files (1284 lines), stripping `creationflags=windows_hide_flags()` from nearly every Windows subprocess spawn in the codebase. Only a handful of files were individually re-fixed since — everything else has been flashing a console window on Windows on every `git`/`npm`/`ssh` subprocess call for months, including on every single CLI/TUI launch via `banner.py`'s startup version check.

**Silent data loss on update:** separately, `hermes update`'s fast-forward-failure path does `git reset --hard origin/<branch>` when local and remote history have diverged, with no backup of the local HEAD first. Any committed-but-unpushed local work is silently discarded. This hit the same user twice in one week before the guard in this PR existed.

## Fix

1. Restores `creationflags=windows_hide_flags()` (or `windows_detach_popen_kwargs()` for long-running detached processes) across every remaining file hit by the June revert: `banner.py` (startup path, highest priority — 7 sites), `cli.py` (24 sites), `kanban_db.py`, `gateway/run.py`, `clipboard.py`, `claw.py`, `mcp_catalog.py`, `dep_ensure.py`, `doctor.py`, `setup.py`, `dump.py`, `gateway/platforms/webhook.py`, `plugins/platforms/raft/adapter.py`, `managed_uv.py`, `plugins/memory/mem0/_setup.py`, `plugins/memory/honcho/client.py`, `agent/proxy_sources/iron_proxy.py`, `tools/environments/docker.py`, `tools/environments/ssh.py`, `hermes_cli/uninstall.py`, `plugins_cmd.py`, `profiles.py`, `agent/secret_sources/{bitwarden,onepassword}.py`, `plugins/platforms/discord/voice_mixer.py`, `scripts/contributor_audit.py`, `profile_distribution.py`. ~60 call sites total.
2. Also fixes `plugins_cmd.py`'s `_run_plugin_git` helper — introduced by a more recent refactor of the plugin-update flow, so it never had the flag to begin with (found while rebasing this branch onto current main).
3. Also fixes `apps/desktop/electron/ssh-connection.ts` (2 unhidden `ssh` spawns for Remote/SSH backend profiles) via `hiddenWindowsChildOptions()`.
4. Adds a safety guard to `hermes update`'s reset path: before `git reset --hard origin/<branch>`, pins current HEAD to a `hermes-local-fixes-backup` branch and prints the recovery command, so committed local work is always recoverable after a forced reset.
5. Also includes a gateway `RestartOnFailure` fix (synchronous `sh.Run` + exit-code propagation) and an MCP `_normalize_headers` fix (headers config coerced to dict before use) that were bundled with the safety-guard commit originally.

## Verification

- Every touched Python file re-parses cleanly (`ast.parse` + `py_compile`).
- Desktop app (`apps/desktop`) rebuilds clean with the restored fixes.
- Live-tested on Windows: flash confirmed gone on affected startup/git paths after rebuild.
- Deliberately left untouched: `service_manager.py` (Linux-only s6-overlay branch), `agent/secret_sources/command.py` (Windows early-return), `agent/anthropic_adapter.py` (Darwin-gated / intentional interactive OAuth), `scripts/profile-tui.py` (imports `pty`, doesn't import on Windows at all), `hermes_cli/relaunch.py` (intentional visible self-relaunch).

Reported and fixed by @Oc2cO.

body:
Closes #281 (primeira metade).

## Causa
Ao perder linha de visão, o bot largava o alvo em **1.2s** sem distinguir **parede** de **fumaça**. Com fumaça (~10s de nuvem), o bot virava roam imediatamente - o \`barata tonta\` do relato - e dois inimigos se cruzavam dentro/atrás da nuvem sem nunca re-engatarem (ambos cegos e sem memória).

## Correção
Enquanto uma **nuvem opaca** bloqueia o segmento bot→alvo (mesmo teste de segmento-esfera do \`_losClear\`), o grace estica **1.2s → 4s**: o bot segura a direção e re-engata no instante em que a fumaça abre. O **gate de tiro (\`_losLost\`) continua fechado** — não atira no que não vê (sem wallhack).

## Validação
- \`botsim 60 fy_pool_day\`: latFlips 9.5 · stuck 4.4% · eff 0.154 — sem regressão de rota vs baseline pós-#226
- BOT2/BOT8 medidos no build do CI

author: pyup-bot
body:
This PR updates [chardet](https://pypi.org/project/chardet) from **3.0.4** to **7.6.0**.



<details>
  <summary>Changelog</summary>
  
  
   ### 7.6.0
   ```
   -------------------

**Performance:**

- Compiled wheels now score bigram profiles through a small Cython
  kernel alongside mypyc, and the pair is 4.7x faster than the pure
  wheel on CPython 3.14.  ``_kernel.py`` stays plain Python (PyPy and
  pure wheels run it interpreted, unchanged), ``_kernel.pxd`` adds C
  types at build time and ships nothing, and detection output is
  bit-identical.  The kernel declares itself safe without the GIL, so
  free-threaded CPython scales instead of silently re-enabling the GIL
  on import: 3.14t runs the whole suite in ~340ms across 8 threads,
  the fastest configuration measured.  Compiled builds now need both
  hooks::

      HATCH_BUILD_HOOK_ENABLE_MYPYC=true HATCH_BUILD_HOOK_ENABLE_CUSTOM=true uv build

  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Added support for CPython 3.15, including the free-threaded build.
  No code changes were needed.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)

**Bug Fixes:**

- Fixed delimited ASCII data like ``|NAME,+LAY|`` misdetecting as
  UTF-7, a follow-up to `371
  <https://github.com/chardet/chardet/issues/371>`_.  Two new checks:
  the whole buffer must actually decode as UTF-7 (``+|`` is an illegal
  shift, so tabular data fails immediately), and a block encoding a
  single code unit must land in a script range where a lone shifted
  character plausibly occurs.  ``+LAY`` decodes to U+2C06, Glagolitic;
  no genuine lone block in the corpus lands anywhere like it, while em
  dashes, ellipses, kanji, and accented letters all pass.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Signed UTF-7 no longer reads as ASCII.  The BOM stage recognizes the
  four UTF-7 signature prefixes (``+/v8-`` and friends) when the rest
  of the buffer decodes as UTF-7 --- the prefix alone is ordinary ASCII
  (a diff of V8 source paths starts with ``+/v8``).  This is a
  deliberate divergence from WHATWG's browser-security exclusion of
  UTF-7: chardet already detects the unsigned form, so refusing only
  the signed one made no sense.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- ``detect()`` no longer returns an encoding that cannot decode the
  input it was given
  (`380 <https://github.com/chardet/chardet/issues/380>`_).  When the
  whole input has been examined and the winner's only multi-byte
  evidence is an incomplete trailing sequence, the best candidate that
  decodes the input completely wins instead.  Genuinely truncated data
  keeps its answer: CJK cut mid-character, or input sliced at
  ``max_bytes``.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Short apostrophe-heavy English is no longer labeled Scottish Gaelic
  or Breton.  A rare-language label on an input under 128 bytes now
  needs a 0.03 lead over the best mainstream language, mirroring the
  encoding-side arbitration in ADR-0005.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Hungarian text no longer loses to a Czech reading: confusion
  rescoring compares tied pairs only under language models both
  encodings have.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Space-padded text no longer matches a degenerate Serbian model at
  high confidence.  Statistical scoring now skips repeated-whitespace
  bigrams, matching the whitespace collapse training already applies.
  Fixed 21 files plus a long-standing GB2312 known failure.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- EBCDIC text is no longer invisible to the early pipeline.  The
  binary stage treats EBCDIC's 0x05/0x15 tab and newline as whitespace
  when the data is high-byte-dominated, and the markup stage reads
  charset declarations through a cp037 decode of the head.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Fixed the last two EBCDIC sibling misdetections: a letter reading
  beating punctuation is no longer evidence by itself, and
  low-confidence near-ties scan deeper but need the category vote and
  the bigram rescore to agree.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Fixed training normalization gaps that starved ISO-8859-16 (legacy
  cedilla forms) and the 26 pre-euro encodings (the euro sign) at
  exactly the bytes that discriminate them from their siblings.
  Cedilla folds to comma-below and the euro to the currency sign
  wherever the target encoding cannot represent them.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)

**Improvements:**

- Retrained every bigram model on a refreshed, deduplicated corpus
  with the ADR-0004 hardening: whitespace collapses after encoding,
  retention guards hard-fail mostly unencodable corpora, Serbian gets
  real Latin-script text, CP1006 gains its sixteen missing Urdu
  letters, and wiki markup is stripped before bigram counting.
  Training provenance is now recorded per model, so test data added
  after a retrain is detectable as such.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- New ANSI-art model.  cp437 detection now includes a profile trained
  on 16,621 text-mode art files from `16colo.rs <https://16colo.rs/>`_,
  keyed under the ``zxx`` pseudo-language and reported with
  ``language=None``.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Rare-language arbitration: a low-confidence statistical winner from a
  language with no documented legacy-encoding population (Scottish
  Gaelic, Welsh, Irish, Breton) yields to a near-tied mainstream
  candidate.  Genuine Celtic text wins by landslides and is unaffected;
  eight boundary sentinels in the test suite guard the gate.  Design
  and evidence in ADR-0005.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Confusion-group resolution is context-aware: votes are counted per
  occurrence, letter readings with no word shape are demoted, and
  art-model wins are exempt.  Fixed twelve EBCDIC and Latin files that
  were riding single-byte coin flips.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Statistical dead heats no longer resolve by candidate enumeration
  order.  Three tiebreaks: prefer the Windows superset, prefer the more
  prevalent era when there is no high-byte evidence, and prefer a
  classic-Mac candidate when line endings are bare ``\r``.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Training pipeline hardening after a cache-loss post-mortem: retrains
  that would silently drop a model now abort loudly, caches filter in
  place instead of being deleted wholesale, and the artpack fetcher
  builds into a temporary directory.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
   ```
   
  
  
   ### 7.5.1
   ```
   -------------------

**Bug Fixes:**

- Fixed markup-declared encodings being reported under a name that can't
  decode the input.  A page declaring ``Shift_JIS`` but using CP932
  extension characters (like ①) came back as ``SHIFT_JIS``, which fails
  ``.decode()`` on those same bytes.  Superset promotion (``CP932``,
  ``CP949``) now always fires when the reported name can't decode the
  data but the superset can.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Fixed a lying charset declaration beating genuine UTF-8 content.  A
  UTF-8 page declaring ``<meta charset="iso-8859-1">`` came back as
  ISO-8859-1, which decodes to mojibake.  Valid multi-byte UTF-8 now
  wins over a conflicting declaration; pure ASCII and real single-byte
  content still honor it.
  (`Dan Blanchard <https://github.com/dan-blanchard>`_ via Claude)
- Fixed BOM-les

author: venkatramanagyambavantha-code
body:
Review feedback on both Kafka cells carried the same note: the Kafka strategy must be explicitly provided rather than inferred, a wrong detection invalidates the run, and the development, architecture, and application teams must be aligned on it before the assessment starts. Both prompts and the machinery that selects between them change together, so the framework never infers a strategy and then hands it to a prompt that rejects inferred strategies.

Shared:

* Both prompts declare `${input:kafkaStrategy}` and run only when the supplied value matches their own strategy, following the `${input:targetDeployment}` precedent on planner-3 and planner-3a
* The Database-to-Kafka Pairing Standard is demoted from selector to cross-check. The database model no longer chooses the prompt; a contradiction between the confirmed model and the supplied strategy is recorded as a finding rather than changing the strategy or blocking
* SKILL.md selects the prompt from the supplied value and asks for it when absent, instead of deriving it from whether Cosmos DB or Azure SQL was confirmed

Active-Active:

Eighteen concern groups become seven areas. Areas 1 through 4 are the required findings: producer topic targeting, consumer read source, the steady-state mirror read control, and Kafka client 3.8 or later, which this prompt did not previously check. Areas 5 through 7 retain application-code consequences of the cutover mechanism itself: duplicate and out-of-order processing across a flag transition, the read source being resolved once at startup so the flag has no runtime effect, and broker addresses learned from advertised.listeners being persisted so reconnection fails.

Active-Standby:

Scope now states that applications connect through DNS rather than region-specific endpoints, with DNS directing traffic by primary and secondary designation and region health. Independent clusters, managed replication, mirror-topic state, offset synchronization, promotion, failover, failback, failure detection, and DNS reset are named as Kafka shared services responsibilities that are never application-code findings.

The twenty-one concern taxonomy becomes eleven. Dropped: failback and regional recovery, cluster-specific credential and trust-store dependencies, cross-region configuration symmetry, and the pairing rule. The Tier A and Tier B branching is removed with it, since it existed only to handle a topology established by inference at varying confidence.

author: jonpulsifer
body:
Deploys Prowler's API, Celery worker, beat scheduler and UI to the offsite cluster as a single first-party chart, authenticating to GCP without a service-account key.

## Why not upstream's charts

Upstream ships four under `contrib/k8s/helm`, and none of them fit:

- `prowler-cli` is hardcoded to `args: ["kubernetes", "-z", "-b"]`, mounts no cloud credential, and writes its output to a directory that vanishes with the pod.
- `prowler-app` is the maintained one, but it pulls in bitnami `postgresql`, valkey.io `valkey` and `neo4j` as subcharts, and its README says the default setup is not production-ready. Its own `_helpers.tpl` also emits no `NEO4J_*` env when `neo4j.enabled: false`, which crash-loops the API rather than disabling the feature.

`packages/charts/prowler` takes the two published images and wires them to what this cluster already runs. It is consumed by path from the `infra` GitRepository like `app` and `ai-agent`, so nothing new gets published.

## Native building blocks

| Need | Used |
| --- | --- |
| Postgres | CloudNativePG `Cluster` |
| Valkey | valkey-operator `ValkeyCluster` |
| Ingress | `cluster-gateway`, new per-hostname listener |
| Secrets | `onepassword-connect` ClusterSecretStore |
| GCP auth | `fml-pool` workload identity federation |

Three constraints drove the shape:

- **Two Postgres roles.** The API migrates and holds `django_*` as an owner, and reads tenant-scoped tables as a least-privilege role under RLS. `managed.roles` adds CREATEROLE to CNPG's bootstrapped owner so the first migration can create the second role, with `passwordSecret` pointed back at `<cluster>-app` so there is one credential rather than two. Superuser is not needed — `pg_trgm` is trusted from PG13 on.
- **Valkey must be single-shard.** Prowler selects logical databases by number (0 broker, 2 SSE bus) and cluster mode does not implement SELECT. Valkey's defaults already provide 16 databases and `noeviction`.
- **Attack Paths cannot be turned off.** The four `NEO4J_*` variables are read at Django settings import with no defaults, and `/health/ready` returns 503 without a reachable graph. It runs on DozerDB because the feature issues `CREATE DATABASE` per tenant, which Neo4j Community Edition does not implement.

## Keyless GCP

`prowler-scanner@homelab-ng` holds no key — `iam.managed.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` is enforced org-wide and managed constraints cannot be overridden below the org, so one could not be minted. The pod projects a ServiceAccount token, the pool exchanges it at STS, and the account is impersonated. Read roles are bound at the organization node so all ten projects inherit them; a custom role carries `storage.buckets.getIamPolicy`, the one permission Viewer omits that the public-access checks need.

Prowler accepts the `external_account` document as a stored provider credential because it hands the value to `google.auth.load_credentials_from_dict`, which dispatches on `type`. That is a property of an unvalidated field rather than a designed feature, so the image is digest-pinned and the chart comments say so.

## Validation

- `helm lint packages/charts/prowler` — pass
- `helm template` + `kubectl apply --dry-run=client` — 13 objects, all valid
- `.github/scripts/render-cluster-apps.sh` — exit 0, templates the chart against the real HelmRelease values
- `tofu validate` on `terraform/gcp/organization` and `terraform/gcp/projects/homelab-ng` — pass

## Before this can serve traffic

1. Create a `prowler` item in the 1Password homelab vault with the eight fields `clusters/offsite/apps/prowler/external-secret.yaml` names. `NEO4J_AUTH` is `neo4j/<neo4j-password>`.
2. Apply the Terraform (org IAM policy is authoritative — read that plan carefully).
3. Onboard providers in the UI. The App scans one Provider row per project: `get_prowler_provider_kwargs` hardcodes `project_ids: [provider.uid]` and there is no `/organizations` endpoint in the OSS API, so org-wide means ten rows in a Provider Group, each holding the same `external_account` document from the `prowler-gcp` ConfigMap. Org-level Viewer already covers all ten.

## Known ceilings

- **Report downloads 404.** The worker writes to `DJANGO_TMP_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY` and the API serves from local disk, which needs RWX; offsite has only `local-path`. Findings in the UI are unaffected — this is the downloadable artifact only. Fixed by the S3 offload vars or an RWX class.
- **`managed.roles` is new to this repo.** Nothing else here uses it, so the CREATEROLE reconcile is the first thing to check on apply.
- **No `roles/cloudasset.viewer`.** That is what `prowler gcp --organization-id` needs to enumerate projects, and the App path does not use it. Add it if a CLI org scan is ever wanted.

author: lvt-eng
body:
🎯 **What:** The FastAPI application was configured with `allow_origins=["*"]`, which is overly permissive. This was fixed by reading the allowed domains from an environment variable `E50_CORS_ALLOW_ORIGIN`, with a safe hardcoded fallback to trusted production (`https://tryonyou.app`) and local development origins (`http://localhost:5173`).

⚠️ **Risk:** Using `*` for CORS origins allows any website to make requests to the API. If cookies/credentials were enabled, it would allow cross-site authenticated requests. Even without credentials, it allows arbitrary websites to read responses from the API, leading to potential data leakage.

🛡️ **Solution:** Restricted the allowed origins by replacing the wildcard with an explicit list loaded from the environment (defaulting to the tryonyou app domain and localhost). Added robust testing (`tests/test_cors_security.py`) to explicitly check that preflight requests from disallowed origins are rejected, returning a 400 status.

author: raymond-nassar
body:
## In plain English

The project keeps a list of planned improvements, roughly ordered by a score that says what is worth
doing next. A note at the end explains the handful of places where that order and the score disagree.
It said there were four such places, and that all the work involved was already finished, so the
order was a record of what had been done rather than a plan for what to do next.

Both halves had gone out of date as more items were added. Counted again from the list itself rather
than by re-reading the sentence, there are six, and three of the items involved have not been done
yet. More usefully, counting neighbouring rows turned out to be the wrong way to ask the question at
all. Someone deciding what to work on next reads only the unfinished rows and skips the rest, so a
finished row sitting between two unfinished ones hides a disagreement completely. Asked that way
there are two, and one of them was invisible to the first method.

The note now names both, and says plainly what it does about them: the score decides, and the order
is left as it is. Re-sorting would move more than a third of the rows, would need doing again the
next time an item was added, and would not change a single decision, because the score already
settles those.

Nothing you can see changes, and nothing you have saved is affected. This is a correction to the
project's own planning notes.

## What changed

`PRODUCT_BACKLOG.md` Appendix B: the opening claim is re-derived and the policy question BL-121 left
open is answered.

| Claim | Was | Is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adjacent pairs where the lower score sits above the higher | four | six |
| Rows involved | eight | twelve |
| How many of them have shipped | all | nine |
| Inversions among rows still to be picked up | not measured | two |

The four items the paragraph named are still four of the six, so it was right about what it named.
It was wrong about what it counted, and the sentence resting the decision on all of them having
shipped was wrong outright.

### The measure that was being used is the wrong one

Six is the count over adjacent table rows. A reader choosing what to do next reads the thirteen rows
still to be picked up and skips the eighty-six that are not, so a shipped row between two open rows
hides an inversion from a scan of neighbours. Thirteen is what the document's own status key at
`PRODUCT_BACKLOG.md:227` means by an item still to be picked up; counting the single `Proposed` row
beside them gives fourteen and leaves both pairs below exactly as they are.

Measured over the open rows alone there are two, and **only one of them appears among the six**:

- `BL-117` at 3.0 sits below `BL-114` at 2.67, four places down with three shipped rows between them.
  The adjacency scan reports this instead as BL-117 against BL-038, which has shipped, so it names a
  disagreement nobody has to choose between and misses the one they do.
- `BL-120` at 2.5 sits below `BL-119` at 2.0.

Filing this item from the whole-table measure alone would have replaced one wrong number with another
and left the live pair unnamed.

### The decision, and why re-sorting was declined

An inversion in an unshipped row is named and the order left alone; the score governs wherever
position and score disagree.

Re-sorting is declined on cost, not on risk. The risk would be figures read off the order going stale
unnoticed, and that is already covered: `checkRanks` and `checkOrdinalHeadings` in
`scripts/check-counts.mjs` rebuild every row's rank from the table and fail a stale one. Sorting the
table and running the gate turns four claims red, all of them in Appendix B, so a re-sort cannot
quietly invalidate anything.

What decides it is cost against nothing gained. A stable sort by score moves **37 of the 99 rows**,
and the six pairs do not reduce to six swaps: exchanging the members of each pair in one pass leaves
six inversions again, because a swap can lift a row above a third one it also outscores. Nothing
gates the order itself, so it would drift again with the next item filed. And the rule above leaves
no decision resting on the order.

The rows sitting out of score order are **four filed in four separate changes**, not a block: BL-117,
BL-118, BL-119 and BL-120 hold four consecutive positions immediately above the two open rows that
were already there, ordered by when they were filed rather than by what they score. Not every recent
row landed that way, which is why this is a habit to note rather than a rule: BL-114 was filed at
2.67 in the same period and sits among the other 2.67 rows.

## Review round

A `code-review` pass raised eight findings, two of them High. All eight were re-derived independently
before being acted on, and all eight held. Every one is fixed.

| # | Finding | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | "the counts gate is what caught it" was false; `checkLedger` is scoped above `## The backlog` and reads none of these figures | Re-attributed. The gate prints the status tallies and reading that print back against the sentence is a habit, not a check. Stated as such. |
| 2 | "nothing derives the figures read off the order" was false, and it was the load-bearing premise | Confirmed false and the argument rebuilt on cost. Sorting the table and running the gate turns exactly four claims red, reproduced here. |
| 3 | Case 1 does not test score against position; all eleven cheaper items also ranked above BL-026 | Confirmed by deriving all eleven ranks. The appendix now says the case is evidence a score beats a label and none that it beats a position. |
| 4 | "ranks this appendix and its own tests cite" was wrong; the tests derive ranks from the live table | Claim removed. Blast radius restated as 37 of 99 rows. |
| 5 | "those fourteen rows" had no antecedent in the appendix | The population is now named and counted where it is introduced. |
| 6 | Fourteen counted the `Proposed` row while the document's key defines still-to-be-picked-up as `Ready` | Adopted the document's own definition: thirteen, against eighty-six. Both pairs survive all four ways of drawing the population. |
| 7 | "a block of six filed after the last sort" was four, filed in four separate changes | Corrected and the four commits named. BL-092 and BL-102 were filed much earlier and sit correctly. |
| 8 | Presenting the open-row count as *the* decision-relevant figure does not survive "the score governs" | Reframed: naming is a courtesy to a reader scanning the order, not what settles the next item. |

The premise in finding 2 also mis-stated the source it cited: `PRODUCT_BACKLOG.md:4691-4694` names two
specific ungated figure shapes *in contrast to four that are gated*, so the sentence generalised those
lines into their opposite. The citation now points at those lines and says what they actually say.

## Verification

**Every figure derived by script over the ranked table, not by reading.** Two independent routes agree
on the whole-table count, and the open-row count is taken separately over `Ready` and over `Ready`
plus `Proposed`, which give the same two pairs.

**The re-sort experiment was run, not assumed.** The table was stable-sorted in place, the counts gate
run against it, and the file restored byte-identical. Result: 37 rows move, exactly four rank claims
turn red, and one pass of local swaps leaves six inversions rather than none.

**The item's own shipping moved one of the figures.** The first draft said fifteen open rows, true of
the tree the measurement ran against and false of the tree it was written into, because marking
BL-123 `Shipped` removes its own row from the population. No gate catches that, which the record now
says plainly.

**The dash scan was proven able to fail.** The scan reported 0, so an em dash and an en dash were
planted in a tracked file and the scan re-run: it caught them, and the file was restored
byte-identical. A first control attempt failed and was itself found faulty, since `Get-Content` piped
into `Ou
